LLM answer not available - showing evidence summary.
- To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere. [F-004]
- According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability. [F-006]
- Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration; in microgravity, convective air flow speed is also critical. [F-007]
- The flammability of solid materials such as fabrics (SIBAL, Nomex) and plastics (PMMA) has been investigated in the BASS, BASS-II, and Saffire-I, -II, -III flight experiments. [F-010]
- Spacecraft fire detection in microgravity has been tested through the SAME and SAME-R (Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment) flight investigations. [F-011]
- BASS-II (golden table, unverified draft): O2 0.136-0.222, pressure 14.388-14.696 psi, same-test lunar match: no
- Conflict [BASS-II | flow_cm_s_max]: up to 40 cm/s (S-030 row 40) vs 53 cm/s (Air display, T17) | ~55 cm/s hardware (S-031 row 117; S-007 p.12; S-005 p.7; S-004 p.3)
- Passages retrieved: [S-007:134], [S-007:130], [S-007:106], [S-007:123], [S-007:108]

facts.claim: To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability.
Flammability depends strongly on oxygen concentration; in microgravity, convective air flow speed is also critical.
The flammability of solid materials such as fabrics (SIBAL, Nomex) and plastics (PMMA) has been investigated in the BASS, BASS-II, and Saffire-I, -II, -III flight experiments.
Spacecraft fire detection in microgravity has been tested through the SAME and SAME-R (Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment) flight investigations.

fields.fuel_shape_size: PMMA rod (6.35-12.7 mm diameter) | thin PMMA film (0.1-0.4 mm; 1-2 cm wide) | thick PMMA slab (1-5 mm) | 4 cm diameter sphere section | SIBAL strip (1.2/2.2 cm × 10 cm)
fields.o2_note: calibrated initial O2 column used (CSA-CP reading with fixed offset correction against the MCA); 5 impossible values in the 'Calibrated final O2' column (1.6, 0.6, 39.1, 0.9, 40.4) excluded
fields.pressure_note: min = measured 99.2 kPa (14.388 psi); max = nominal 1 atm (14.696 psi); a combination of measured and nominal values
fields.flow_raw: Air display 0 … 53 (T17) | hardware: ~55 cm/s with no restrictors, ~35 cm/s with two restrictors
fields.flow_note: Air display has a ~1 min response time; row 63 (O13a) fan values are in the wrong column — excluded; 0 = flow off (explicit value in the source). The max of 53 comes only from T17, whose cell reads '6   53' (also '6→53' in S-004 p.9), most likely a 6→53 cm/s ramp; every other row is ≤ 15 cm/s — verify by hand
fields.gravity_regime: microgravity | normal (1-g and 5.18 s drop tower comparison)
fields.hardware: MSG: BASS/SPICE flow duct (7.6 × 7.6 × 17 cm), variable-speed fan, flow restrictors, hot-wire igniter, N2 nozzle; N2 dilution of the MSG work volume
fields.lunar_note: O2 upper bound 0.222 < 0.30; pressure lower bound 14.388 psi > 10.2
fields.main_finding: A 1/4-inch PMMA rod that blows off at 16% O2 in 1-g burned steadily at 13.6% O2 on the ISS; the source interprets this as a negative safety margin of −2.4% O2 and states that normal-gravity flammability limits should be lowered. None of the three Nomex samples ignited.

[BASS-II | S-007: NASA/TM-20210011385 BASS-II Summary Report | D.5 Analysis]
The maximum burn time is assumed to be the 2.5-min growth phase plus the 28-min sample
regression phase, for a total of 30.5 min, as plotted in Figure D.5. The maximum temperatures reported in
the following information are for this maximum burn time. The heat release in the early phase is dominated by the ignition energy. Once the combustion heat
release approaches steady state, the igniter is turned off and the flame is sustained. The maximum temperature will occur in the exhaust hardware. This metal (primarily copper)
hardware is built to take the hot combustion gases and cool via conduction to the other hardware. The
maximum temperature if all of the combustion energy is only deposited in this heat sink under these
worst-case assumptions, is 434 °C, which is below the melting point of the lowest melting material
(aluminum at 660 °C) so this absolute worst-case maximum temperature will not cause damage to the
hardware. This maximum temperature will not be realized in actuality because the heat will quickly
dissipate to the main housing, which reaches a maximum temperature of 110 °C if all of the heat is
distributed only there. The experiment assembly dissipates the heat further, and the maximum
temperature of the entire experiment assembly is 62 °C. During the 10-min cooldown for these thick samples, both the flow through the BASS duct and the
MSG air circulation fans help dissipate the heat.

[BASS-II | S-007: NASA/TM-20210011385 BASS-II Summary Report | D.5 Analysis]
D.5 Analysis
As can be seen in Figure D.2, the base of the flame (at x = 0) has the highest burning rate and there is
an exponential decay in the regression rate away from that peak burning rate. Using peak regression rate
(r ) for the four flow profiles given, we can extrapolate down to the 30-cm/s flow of interest. max
The exposed base of the flame (the upstream most point) will be the strongest part of the flame, and
the burning rate is expected to be a maximum there. Based on data in the Section D.7 from a 1-cm-sphere
BASS test, we estimate the regression rate to be 3.05 mm/min, which is in keeping with the estimates
from Figure D.2, as shown in Figure D.3. The downstream regression rates will decay exponentially from
there, as shown in Figure D.2.

[BASS-II | S-007: NASA/TM-20210011385 BASS-II Summary Report | 7.1.4 Results and Discussion]
Figure 7.4.—Steady flame spread rate for both 2.2- and 1.2-cm-wide samples. Figure 7.5 shows a typical flame quenching sequence in the BASS–II experiment. A 2.2-cm-wide
sample in 18.7 percent O was first ignited at 10-cm/s flow. Flow speed was decreased to 2.2 cm/s incrementally after ignition. Figure 7.6 shows flame tracking and flow speed versus time. After ignition,
the flame started to grow. As the flow speed was reduced, both flame length and flame width dropped
accordingly with flow. After 25 s, flow velocity was reduced to 2.2 cm/s and held there for the remainder
of the test. As shown in Figure 7.5, both the flame length and flame width continued to decrease
approaching a circular-shaped blue flame seen from the top. The size of the flame continues to shrink
until extinction is reached. This is typical in a quenching extinction sequence. As the quenching limit is
approached (in this case by turning down the flow velocity), the fuel pyrolysis rate and combustion heat
release rate (HRR) are reduced, and radiation loss becomes a significant fraction of the HRR from the
shrinking flame. When the flame becomes small enough, conduction becomes the additional heat loss. The postburn photo of the sample in Figure 7.5 shows the narrowing of the burnt region as the flame
shrinks toward extinction with a substantial part of the fuel left unburnt along the two sides of the sample
holder. Although this is a concurrently spreading flame, the quenching sequence shows similar
characteristics in opposed flow (Ref.

conflicts.rationale: highest measured value in the table (T17 cell reads '6   53', likely a 6→53 ramp; all other rows ≤ 15 cm/s); 40 appears copied from the BASS-I text — verify T17 by hand

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
